### `libgit2/src/util/strnlen.h` wave 225 batch 0: `p_strnlen`

The campaign's first `port` batch outside the foundational modules. `src/util/strnlen.h` is a
header with no translation unit, and on this build its one item is `#define p_strnlen
strnlen`, libc's; the `GIT_INLINE` body over `memchr` is compiled only under `NO_STRNLEN`,
which no variant defines. `mac::p_strnlen` is the native `const fn strnlen(&[u8]) -> usize`
in `src/libgit2/src/util/strnlen_h.rs`, over `CStr::from_bytes_until_nul` (core's `memchr`),
the pointer and its bound one slice; its docs name the `NO_STRNLEN` branch, which computes
the same length. The file holds no unsafe region and carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. No C
reaches it and the macro has no export: it stays in its header for `alloc.c`, `index.c`,
`midx.c` and `refdb_reftable.c`, which expand it to libc's `strnlen`. libc's `strnlen` takes
its recommended `std` route; nothing of its state crosses to C. The `loc` cell is wavefront's
`query dag --loc`, `0` for a macro.

Tests: six `unit_pub` tests (empty bound, first NUL, no NUL within the bound, bytes past
ASCII, every NUL position in every bound up to 70 bytes from each start within a word, and
`const` evaluation), a doctest, and two `equiv` tests comparing the port with the C's
expansion through `git__strndup` (`StrFree::dup_prefix`), which copies `p_strnlen(s, n)`
bytes. The module has no C tests to carry over.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave
tip `50c93dd23` and on this tree, each suite alone, and read with `report.py` (`C=@c` over the
`coverage` variant's `libcrustify.a`, 89,080 lines, and Rust over the scratch tree's `src/`),
the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`. `report.py`'s scope check fails from the
repository's root, since `llvm-cov` prints rows relative to their common prefix
(`crustify/evolution/coverage-report-relative-rows`); it was run from the scratch tree's
`src/libgit2`. The archive is the 2026-11-13 tree's, so `C LoC` and the Coverage stats
percentages move from the recorded figures, which were measured on the earlier archive and
method; the pp cells are against this run's own tip measurement. The tip's `unit` count was
902, not the recorded 900. The C suites' shifts, `+0.04` pp in `ub_safe` and `-0.02` pp in
`unit`, which this batch's tests do not run, are run-to-run variation. Worklist: Rust
`strnlen_h.rs` 5 of 5 lines, 5 of 5 regions and 1 of 1 function; C `git__strndup`'s
`p_strnlen` line reached 109k times by `equiv`; `strnlen` itself is glibc's, outside the
archive. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+7`) and
`code.tests.loc.total` (`+100`).

The safety audit scans (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the raw
bindings being the crate's own `sys` module since 2026-11-13, the 13 seams with `into_raw`,
`--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`, no export feature in the manifest) move only the line
totals; the boundary scan's sites hold none in the changeset. `ffimap api` against the tip,
with ffibox's private rustdoc JSON (nightly `2026-10-08`): `mac::p_strnlen` is `new`, and
every unattributed module `kept`.

Gates, on the base `50c93dd23`, which the wave branch still pointed at when the batch landed:
the workspace is formatted, and `clippy --all-targets` passes with warnings denied on
`plain`. The whole workspace passes on `plain` (`lib` 840 and 1 ignored, `ub_safe` 762,
`ub_unsafe` 120, `equiv` 528, `unit_pub` 67, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 72 merged and 378 standalone). The module's tests pass
under ASan+UBSan, and the six unit tests under Miri; the two `equiv` tests were each run alone
there and stop at `git_libgit2_init` (`calls libgit2`). The coverage runs ran every suite of
both trees on the nightly; only the known `CommitBuilder` compile-fail doctest fails, on both.
TSan and BSan have no obligation: the batch adds no unsafe code, no `Send` or `Sync` claim and
no thread. No raw binding or C changed, so the packaging gate does not apply. Usage cells are
the assistant's.

### `libgit2/src/util/strnlen.h` wave 225 batch 1: module pass

The module pass, and the module's only review, over batch 0's three paths, for every objective
with `fix`. It files no finding. `strnlen` is `p_strnlen`'s length for every input: the slice
is the pointer and its bound, and `CStr::from_bytes_until_nul` is core's `memchr`, a byte loop
below 16 bytes and word-wise above, as the docs say. It is `const`, safe and anchored
`Replaces` `mac::p_strnlen` with its alias, and no Rust in the crate counts a bounded length by
hand. The equivalence tests reach C's expansion through `git__strndup`, which `StrFree::dup_prefix`
calls on its own copy of the bytes. No C test references the macro, and the ownership store
holds nothing on it. Porting the macro once is sound under `porting-symbols`' Macros section:
the body computes on its arguments alone, both branches give the same length, and libc's
`strnlen` takes its `std` route. The pass adds that evidence to
`crustify/evolution/config-branches-of-one-result`, which stays open.

Gates ran on `end-gates` snapshots under the worktree's `crustify/tmp/`, at 48 jobs, the four
`indexer.c` BSan skips checked against each binary's `--list`. On the wave tip `7ef895eb2`:
plain passes the whole workspace (`lib` 840, `equiv` 528, `ub_safe` 762, `ub_unsafe` 120,
`unit_pub` 67, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 72 and 378). ASan+UBSan and TSan pass it too, except
the known `compile_fail` snapshots and the `CommitBuilder` doctest. Miri passes every binary
(`lib` 392, `ub_safe` 194, `equiv` 38, `unit_pub` 32, `ub_unsafe` 19 passed, the rest marked).
BSan passes `lib` 833, `ub_safe` 757, `ub_unsafe` 120 and `hidden_symbols`, but times out at
5400 s on `unit_pub` and `equiv`, each on one of this module's sweeps,
`every_nul_position_in_every_bound` and `every_nul_position_matches_the_c`, every other test of
both having passed. Alone, the `unit_pub` sweep kept one core busy as its memory grew about
8 MB/s: BorrowSanitizer's cost per access to one buffer grows with its borrow history (its
second word offset took 420 s against the first's 90 s, flat at 103 s with a buffer per offset;
`crustify/evolution/bsan-borrow-history-grows`). The fix, `095f69596`, gives each offset its
own buffer, and under `cfg(bsan)` sweeps bounds up to 24 bytes, past `memchr`'s 16. Every other
build sweeps to 70. On `095f69596` plain, ASan+UBSan, TSan and Miri give the tip's results,
and BSan passes `unit_pub` (67, 71 s) and `equiv` (519, 8 ignored under BSan as before, the
indexer skip, 3246 s). The diff touches those two binaries' test files alone, so BSan's other
binaries keep the tip's results.

The safety audit scan (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, flags as batch 0's) differs from batch 0's only in
`code.tests.loc.total` (`+2`), which moves the Overview's tests LoC. `ffimap api`: `src/` is
unchanged from the tip, so one rustdoc JSON (nightly `2026-10-08`, ffibox's with private items)
serves both sides: `mac::p_strnlen` and every unattributed module are `kept`. Coverage was not
measured again: only the BSan build runs the tests differently, and the coverage cells stand as
batch 0 measured them. No raw binding or C changed, so the packaging gate does not apply.

Proposals: `bsan-sized-tests` (testing-gates: a test BSan cannot finish is sized for it, on
crustify's `libgit2-crustify/evolution/bsan-sized-tests` at `6336c30`, awaiting review) and
`bsan-borrow-history-grows` (BorrowSanitizer, upstream, with its reproducer). Usage cells are
the assistant's.

### `libgit2/src/util/strnlen.h` integrated (2026-11-13)

The pilot of the harness for `port` modules: wave 225's translation batch and module pass ran as
processes of their own through `providers/claude/spawn.py`, on `claude-opus-5-5` through
OpenRouter under `api` billing (`46f68906e`). The module is integrated as `30176475c`; its switch
changes no C, the header having no translation unit, export or tied C test. Usage: batch 0
`$5.42`, `13.67M`, `19m47s`; the module pass `$9.34`, `19.72M`, `3h34m56s`, most of it two
rounds of BSan over the workspace, the first lost to a 5400 s timeout. From 2026-11-13 BSan runs
over the workspace only before a ship point, and otherwise on small things (`990d7033a`,
`22ace3a00`). `Module stats` gains the module's row, the first of a per-TU module: the
foundational modules have none there, so its `Σ` rows hold the legacy modules and this one.


### `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` wave 194 batch 0: `llhttp.c`'s types ahead of api.c

A wrap batch ahead of its consumer: `deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s five types, which api.c's
`port` waves use, bound in llhttp.c's own file, `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`, which
its wave 238 ports. `st::llhttp__internal_s` is `Parser`, a `define_ctype!` layout with
`ParserRef` and `ParserMut`, and its typedefs `llhttp__internal_t`, `llhttp_t` and
`git_http_parser` are the aliases `InternalT`, `LlhttpT` and `HttpParser`. A parser owns
nothing and C keeps no pointer to one, so it is a plain value: `CZeroable`, with no owner or
policy; its constructor, `llhttp__internal_init` through `llhttp_init`, is the next batch's.
The closed enums `llhttp_errno`, `llhttp_method`, `llhttp_status` and `llhttp_type` are
`Errno`, `Method`, `Status` and `ParserType`, 185 variants over bindgen's constants with
fallible conversions and an `Unnamed*` error each, their typedefs aliases (`ErrnoT`, …).

The `fields` cell counts the 21 assigned. 15 have accessors: the fields api.c, http.c,
`transports/httpclient.c` and `transports/httpparser.c` touch. The other six, `_index`,
`_span_pos0`, `_span_cb0`, `_current`, `header_state` and `initial_message_completed`, only
llhttp.c's generated code reads or writes (`query structs --field-touchers`), and three of
them would send it through a wild pointer or out of a table if written from outside, so they
have none (`crustify/evolution/wrap-ahead-field-users`). The fields holding an enum's value
are read typed and fallibly, and raw (`*_raw`) as api.c's getters return them; the flag words
and `finish` raw, until `llhttp_flags`, `llhttp_lenient_flags` and `llhttp_finish` are bound.
`reason` is lent as a `&CStr` for the handle's borrow and set only from a `&'static CStr`;
`error_pos` is never followed, only compared with a caller's slice (`error_offset`); `data`
and `settings` are read as addresses and set through the batch's two `unsafe fn`s, whose
contracts carry what the callbacks read through them. Those four are the boundary scan's
sites in the changeset: no safe form replaces a user's untyped context, and `settings`'
typed getter waits for `llhttp_settings_s`, api.c's item, which the cycle through
`llhttp_cb` puts after this batch (T3 drops the cast edge). The pointer findings of the
struct's eight pointer fields, and `llhttp__internal_init`'s and `llhttp_init`'s `init`
roles, are in the ownership store.

The raw bindings gain `llhttp.h` in `wrapper.h`, the five types with their typedefs, and
api.c's `llhttp_init`, `llhttp_settings_init`, `llhttp_execute` and nine getters, which the
equivalence tests compare with; `llhttp_settings_s` and the callback typedefs come in with
them. Tests: 12 `unit_pub` (the enums' values and errors, every setter against its getter),
4 `ub_safe` (reborrows, a lent reason, parsers moved in a `Vec`), 6 `ub_unsafe` (one suite
per `unsafe` setter: callbacks reading the stored context through C, a context replaced
between calls, NULL settings, a table that ignores `data`), 8 `equiv` (two parsers fed the
same input by `llhttp_execute`, one read through api.c's getters and one through the
handles, compared after every step: a response in pieces, an unnamed status, requests with
their method and upgrade, an invalid message, a callback's own error, a pause and resume, the
lenient flags, the setters' effect on the C) and 5 compile-fail doctests. llhttp has no C
tests of its own in the tree.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave
tip `2216b0cd0` and on this tree, each suite alone, and read with `report.py` from the
scratch tree's `src/libgit2`, the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`. The tip's Rust
figures are the recorded ones; its C figures read `27.92`% (`ub_safe`), `19.08`%
(`ub_unsafe`), `42.51`% (`equiv`), `31.37`% (unit) and `44.98`% (total), against which the pp
cells are taken. The C total moves
by `+1.12` pp: the equivalence and unsafe-setter tests run llhttp's parser, which nothing
reached before (`llhttp.c` 18.64% of lines, `http.c` 78.35%, `api.c` 11.99%). Worklist:
`llhttp.rs` 110 of 110 lines, 33 of 33 functions, 147 of 148 regions; the region missed,

measurement. Of the parser's states the tests reach the initialised, parsing, paused,

`llhttp_execute` make. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+919`)
and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+683`); `wrapped types` counts the five against the recorded
`258`.

The safety audit scans (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the 13 seams,

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Setup

### Setup › Provisioning

CodeQL and wavefront's query pack dependencies are installed, as its README describes.
`crustify/.gitignore` lists `wavefront/codeql` and `wavefront/.cache`.

### Setup › Artifact tree

`crustify/wavefront/` is scaffolded for wavefront's state.

### Setup › Baseline

Once the builds and the baseline are recorded, the CodeQL database is created from a
traced build of the `plain` configuration in a fresh scratch dir, with `c/` as its source
root, and its T1/T2 tables are extracted, through a bootstrap configuration in
`crustify/tmp/`; the campaign's own configuration is the plan's.

## Planning

Planning reads `docs/scoping.md`, `docs/graph.md`, `docs/batching.md`,
`docs/type-lifecycle.md`, `docs/artifacts/t3.md` and `docs/artifacts/schedule.md`.

### Decomposition › Runs

Each planner run brings the configuration and the T3 tables up to date with the plan: it
emits what is missing, migrates what follows an earlier wavefront schema, adds what the
scope adds and corrects what is wrong. A changed configuration or T3 row changes the graph,
so the `todo` waves whose batches it moves are re-planned, and the `depends_on` in
`modules.json` when it moves them.

### Decomposition › Dependencies

The configuration's `modules` are authored from `modules.json`: each module's files, with
the entities its `items` list select, each by the kind it is in C. Wavefront refuses an
entry that claims what its file only declares, and a unit two modules claim, so that every
entity is owned by exactly one module; the configuration is verified against the CLI.
<!-- TODO: wavefront makes a unit of every macro an installed header defines, but of an
internal header's macro only where the closure's code expands it, so an internal API macro
no C of the closure expands is planned nowhere, and it makes units of the configuration and
attribute macros the closure expands too. It has yet to make units of the macros that are
API, and only those, count enums and
macros in the modules' records, and tell a closed enum from a flags one, which the planner
judges until then, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes. -->

A module's dependency records are counted from a schedule of the whole closure, without
`schedule_seeds`: its module record's `depends_on` gives its in-tree records, with their
`unique_edges` and `total_edges`; its items give the `counters`, and their references
whose `scope` is `external` the out-of-tree records.

### Decomposition › Foundational modules

The foundational modules' candidates are selected from the configuration's graph, after
the T3 tables are written, so that their cast edges resolve type-erased values: the
type-erased units that no cast edge ties to a named type, and the units whose pointers
carry the `string` property, that depend on no other module's types. Each candidate's body
is read before it is admitted. Each member's lifecycle role is identified as
`docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes and submitted to the ownership store, so that the bindings of
the foundational modules find it.

### Scheduling › Order

The link units and modules are ordered from the configuration, after its T3 tables are
written, and reviewed there:

- every type-erased parameter and field with no cast, followed until it is read as a named
  type, stored, returned or lost. A hop that dispatches on a tag and reads different types
  per branch establishes none of them;
- every cast edge wavefront derives between two public types, each that is no type
  relation dropped;
- every public type in a cast relation, the pairs that are a hierarchy recorded as
  `base_derived` rows; and
- the type-minting macros, the source checked for invocations that conditional
  compilation hides from the traced build.

A row wavefront warns is stale is corrected or deleted.

### Scheduling › Waves and batches

- A planner run schedules once, its `schedule_seeds` the files
  of the modules it plans, without batch caps: the waves' batches are packed when each
  starts. The output is written to `crustify/tmp/`, never over `schedule.json`.
- A wrap campaign schedules over the API headers alone, in wavefront's API mode.
- A unit wavefront warns belongs to no module, and a module it warns claims no unit, are
  gaps in the decomposition, corrected before the schedule is used.
- Wavefront's `modules` become `schedule.json`'s, each named back to its `link_unit`,
  `module` and `foundational`, with its `layer`, its waves and its dependency records. Its
  `depends_on.external` records group its units' references whose `scope` is `external`
  by the library whose installed headers define the referenced entity, as
  `dependencies.json` names it; the external entity's own dependencies, which wavefront
  walks too, are the side campaign's to schedule.
- Wavefront numbers its waves from 0 in every run, so the `todo` waves are numbered after
  the highest index of a started wave, in wavefront's order, their `depends_on`
  renumbered. A wave's `items` are those of its wavefront batches, with their `home`, their
  `objective`, their `used_fields` as `field_users`, a macro's `type_generator_for`
  deciding its route, and their release points. An item a started wave holds, or that a
  batch has landed with that objective, is dropped, and a dependency on it is one on that
  wave.

### Scheduling › Wrap batches

The units a batch's items depend on are their `depends_on` in the planner run's schedule,
or wavefront's dependency query over them. A wrap batch's items are closed over their wrap
dependencies by that query in API mode, less what
`scheduling`'s Wrap batches section leaves out.

### Scheduling › Later stages

A port campaign's schedule, which is not in API mode, gives each item its release
points, which `schedule.json`'s items carry as wavefront records them, and which place its
later stages: `opaque_after` a `port/layout`, `memory_unmanaged_after` a `port/memory` and
`unreferenced_after` a `port/unexport`; a macro's or a typedef's places none. A stage's
wave waits for the last waves of the modules its point's `closure.modules` names, less the
item's own; with none left, the stage is not planned, unless C tests still reference the
export once the item's module has switched, as the `scheduling` skill's Later stages
section describes. The C tests, which the closure leaves out, hold
no stage back: a `port/unexport` carries over those that still reference its export, as the
`scheduling` skill's Later stages section describes. Whether a user stays C is read from
the whole list of its users, as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section queries them.
`memory_unmanaged_after` is `null` until the ownership store holds the raw roles, so they
are established first.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

#### Lifecycle (`lifecycle`)

Lifecycles submitted to wavefront that are incomplete: a releaser, disposer, cloner or
constructor that the findings of the batches that bound or ported items of the type
route, or items of the foundational modules, missed, checked against the lifecycle
primitives `docs/type-lifecycle.md` identifies.

#### The submitted findings

Whatever the objectives, a review checks the pointer findings an earlier run submitted for
the workset: ownership, access, nullability, cardinality and keepalive. A wrong inference
is a finding.

#### Unsafety

The plan cuts the cycles between modules and types. A raw pointer that stands in for a
dependency a later scheduled batch wraps is such a cut, not an `unsafety` finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A finding on wavefront's findings is filed in its own `<slug>` directory, with its report
and the evidence that proves the submitted finding wrong or incomplete, under:

- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/ownership/`, for a wrong pointer-related inference; or
- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/lifecycle/`, for an incomplete lifecycle.

A defect in wavefront itself is no finding on its findings: it is a proposal, as any tool
defect is.

### Reviewing › Fixes

Under `fix`, each corrected or completed set of findings is submitted again, and a completed lifecycle gets the representations the Rust is missing.

### Reviewing › Plan corrections

A correction of wavefront's planning artifacts is filed in the reviews sub-directory of
what it amends:

- `crustify/reviews/planner/modules/` for a configuration, with the `modules.json`
  finding it follows from;
- `crustify/reviews/planner/chased-casts/` for `chased_casts.csv`: for each `add` row the
  chain followed, hop by hop with `file:line`, or the hop that breaks it; for each `drop`
  row the cast sites that derive the edge, and why they are no type relation; and
- `crustify/reviews/planner/type-generators/` for `type_generators.csv`: the macro's
  invocation sites, conditional ones included, and the shapes they mint.

A report on a T3 table also states the DAG change the edit makes.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.

  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Setup

### Setup › Provisioning

CodeQL and wavefront's query pack dependencies are installed, as its README describes.
`crustify/.gitignore` lists `wavefront/codeql` and `wavefront/.cache`.

### Setup › Artifact tree

`crustify/wavefront/` is scaffolded for wavefront's state.

### Setup › Baseline

Once the builds and the baseline are recorded, the CodeQL database is created from a
traced build of the `plain` configuration in a fresh scratch dir, with `c/` as its source
root, and its T1/T2 tables are extracted, through a bootstrap configuration in
`crustify/tmp/`; the campaign's own configuration is the plan's.

## Planning

Planning reads `docs/scoping.md`, `docs/graph.md`, `docs/batching.md`,
`docs/type-lifecycle.md`, `docs/artifacts/t3.md` and `docs/artifacts/schedule.md`.

### Decomposition › Runs

Each planner run brings the configuration and the T3 tables up to date with the plan: it
emits what is missing, migrates what follows an earlier wavefront schema, adds what the
scope adds and corrects what is wrong. A changed configuration or T3 row changes the graph,
so the `todo` waves whose batches it moves are re-planned, and the `depends_on` in
`modules.json` when it moves them.

### Decomposition › Dependencies

The configuration's `modules` are authored from `modules.json`: each module's files, with
the entities its `items` list select, each by the kind it is in C. Wavefront refuses an
entry that claims what its file only declares, and a unit two modules claim, so that every
entity is owned by exactly one module; the configuration is verified against the CLI.
<!-- TODO: wavefront makes a unit of every macro an installed header defines, but of an
internal header's macro only where the closure's code expands it, so an internal API macro
no C of the closure expands is planned nowhere, and it makes units of the configuration and
attribute macros the closure expands too. It has yet to make units of the macros that are
API, and only those, count enums and
macros in the modules' records, and tell a closed enum from a flags one, which the planner
judges until then, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes. -->

A module's dependency records are counted from a schedule of the whole closure, without
`schedule_seeds`: its module record's `depends_on` gives its in-tree records, with their
`unique_edges` and `total_edges`; its items give the `counters`, and their references
whose `scope` is `external` the out-of-tree records.

### Decomposition › Foundational modules

The foundational modules' candidates are selected from the configuration's graph, after
the T3 tables are written, so that their cast edges resolve type-erased values: the
type-erased units that no cast edge ties to a named type, and the units whose pointers
carry the `string` property, that depend on no other module's types. Each candidate's body
is read before it is admitted. Each member's lifecycle role is identified as
`docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes and submitted to the ownership store, so that the bindings of
the foundational modules find it.

### Scheduling › Order

The link units and modules are ordered from the configuration, after its T3 tables are
written, and reviewed there:

- every type-erased parameter and field with no cast, followed until it is read as a named
  type, stored, returned or lost. A hop that dispatches on a tag and reads different types
  per branch establishes none of them;
- every cast edge wavefront derives between two public types, each that is no type
  relation dropped;
- every public type in a cast relation, the pairs that are a hierarchy recorded as
  `base_derived` rows; and
- the type-minting macros, the source checked for invocations that conditional
  compilation hides from the traced build.

A row wavefront warns is stale is corrected or deleted.

### Scheduling › Waves and batches

- A planner run schedules once, its `schedule_seeds` the files
  of the modules it plans, without batch caps: the waves' batches are packed when each
  starts. The output is written to `crustify/tmp/`, never over `schedule.json`.
- A wrap campaign schedules over the API headers alone, in wavefront's API mode.
- A unit wavefront warns belongs to no module, and a module it warns claims no unit, are
  gaps in the decomposition, corrected before the schedule is used.
- Wavefront's `modules` become `schedule.json`'s, each named back to its `link_unit`,
  `module` and `foundational`, with its `layer`, its waves and its dependency records. Its
  `depends_on.external` records group its units' references whose `scope` is `external`
  by the library whose installed headers define the referenced entity, as
  `dependencies.json` names it; the external entity's own dependencies, which wavefront
  walks too, are the side campaign's to schedule.
- Wavefront numbers its waves from 0 in every run, so the `todo` waves are numbered after
  the highest index of a started wave, in wavefront's order, their `depends_on`
  renumbered. A wave's `items` are those of its wavefront batches, with their `home`, their
  `objective`, their `used_fields` as `field_users`, a macro's `type_generator_for`
  deciding its route, and their release points. An item a started wave holds, or that a
  batch has landed with that objective, is dropped, and a dependency on it is one on that
  wave.

### Scheduling › Wrap batches

The units a batch's items depend on are their `depends_on` in the planner run's schedule,
or wavefront's dependency query over them. A wrap batch's items are closed over their wrap
dependencies by that query in API mode, less what
`scheduling`'s Wrap batches section leaves out.

### Scheduling › Later stages

A port campaign's schedule, which is not in API mode, gives each item its release
points, which `schedule.json`'s items carry as wavefront records them, and which place its
later stages: `opaque_after` a `port/layout`, `memory_unmanaged_after` a `port/memory` and
`unreferenced_after` a `port/unexport`; a macro's or a typedef's places none. A stage's
wave waits for the last waves of the modules its point's `closure.modules` names, less the
item's own; with none left, the stage is not planned, unless C tests still reference the
export once the item's module has switched, as the `scheduling` skill's Later stages
section describes. The C tests, which the closure leaves out, hold
no stage back: a `port/unexport` carries over those that still reference its export, as the
`scheduling` skill's Later stages section describes. Whether a user stays C is read from
the whole list of its users, as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section queries them.
`memory_unmanaged_after` is `null` until the ownership store holds the raw roles, so they
are established first.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

#### Lifecycle (`lifecycle`)

Lifecycles submitted to wavefront that are incomplete: a releaser, disposer, cloner or
constructor that the findings of the batches that bound or ported items of the type
route, or items of the foundational modules, missed, checked against the lifecycle
primitives `docs/type-lifecycle.md` identifies.

#### The submitted findings

Whatever the objectives, a review checks the pointer findings an earlier run submitted for
the workset: ownership, access, nullability, cardinality and keepalive. A wrong inference
is a finding.

#### Unsafety

The plan cuts the cycles between modules and types. A raw pointer that stands in for a
dependency a later scheduled batch wraps is such a cut, not an `unsafety` finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A finding on wavefront's findings is filed in its own `<slug>` directory, with its report
and the evidence that proves the submitted finding wrong or incomplete, under:

- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/ownership/`, for a wrong pointer-related inference; or
- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/lifecycle/`, for an incomplete lifecycle.

A defect in wavefront itself is no finding on its findings: it is a proposal, as any tool
defect is.

### Reviewing › Fixes

Under `fix`, each corrected or completed set of findings is submitted again, and a completed lifecycle gets the representations the Rust is missing.

### Reviewing › Plan corrections

A correction of wavefront's planning artifacts is filed in the reviews sub-directory of
what it amends:

- `crustify/reviews/planner/modules/` for a configuration, with the `modules.json`
  finding it follows from;
- `crustify/reviews/planner/chased-casts/` for `chased_casts.csv`: for each `add` row the
  chain followed, hop by hop with `file:line`, or the hop that breaks it; for each `drop`
  row the cast sites that derive the edge, and why they are no type relation; and
- `crustify/reviews/planner/type-generators/` for `type_generators.csv`: the macro's
  invocation sites, conditional ones included, and the shapes they mint.

A report on a T3 table also states the DAG change the edit makes.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.

content.content:
# Wavefront

Wavefront analyzes a C codebase and schedules its units in dependency order
for translation to Rust. It extracts entities and dependencies with CodeQL,
builds a cycle-free dependency graph of the codebase's types and symbols, and
packs that graph into ordered waves of batches. Each batch can be translated
once the waves before it are complete.

Wavefront keeps its analysis simple: it infers facts from the codebase without
data-flow or points-to analysis. It is built for neuro-symbolic workflows, in
which human or LLM reasoning complements its static facts. You can state the
polymorphic and type-erased edges it cannot infer; Wavefront loads them into
the dependency graph, and its schedules order units by them. You can also
record pointer-level ownership and lifecycle properties for each type and
symbol, which Wavefront returns with their records.

## Requirements

- Python 3.13 or newer
- The [CodeQL CLI](https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries), on `PATH`

## Installation

```sh
git clone https://github.com/crustify-rs/wavefront.git
cd wavefront
python -m pip install -e .
codeql pack install src/
```

## Usage

```text
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH COMMAND ...
```

`REPO_ROOT` is the root of the C repository. `--config` names its
`wavefront-config.json`; a relative path is resolved from `REPO_ROOT`.

### Configuration

```json
{
  "state_dir": ".wavefront",
  "closure": {
    "impl_files": {"included": ["src/"], "excluded": ["src/tests/"]},
    "api_headers": {"included": ["include/widget.h"]}
  },
  "modules": [
    {"name": "src/mem.c", "files": ["src/mem.c", "src/mem.h"]},
    {"name": "src/widget.c", "files": ["src/widget.c", "include/widget.h"]}
  ],
  "schedule_seeds": ["include/widget.h"],
  "t3_dir": "t3"
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state_dir` | Directory for the CodeQL database and tables, ownership findings, and caches. |
| `closure` | The program Wavefront analyzes, for its graph, queries and usage counts: `impl_files`, the sources and private headers that implement it, and `api_headers`, the headers that publish its API, each `included` files and directories, less what `excluded` matches. See [Files](docs/scoping.md#files). |
| `modules` | Optional. Module records, `{name, files}`, each file entry as in `schedule_seeds`: a module is a named group of files and items, typically a TU with its headers, unrelated to C++20 modules. A schedule orders each module's units together, the modules in dependency order with their cycles cut. A unit no module claims is ordered alone. See [Modules](docs/scoping.md#modules). |
| `schedule_seeds` | Optional. What `wavefront schedule` starts from: a list of file entries, each seeding what its file defines or declares; a schedule holds its seeds and what they depend on. A file entry is a path, a directory written with a trailing slash, or `{path, items}` whose `included` and `excluded` items, each `{name, kind}`, narrow what it seeds. Without it, every unit of the closure. See [Schedule seeds](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds). |
| `t3_dir` | Optional. Directory, relative to `state_dir`, holding the T3 tables ([`examples/t3/`](examples/t3/)). |

Paths are relative to `REPO_ROOT`. A trailing slash selects a directory
recursively, in `included` and `excluded` alike; `excluded` is optional. See [`examples/wavefront-config.json`](examples/wavefront-config.json).

### 1. Extract

Build the project under CodeQL, then extract the T1 (entity) and T2 (edge)
tables into `<state_dir>/codeql/`:

```sh
codeql database create REPO_ROOT/.wavefront/codeql/db \
  --language=cpp --source-root=REPO_ROOT --command="make -j"
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config wavefront-config.json extract-ql
```

Run `extract-ql` again only when the database changes.

### 2. Query

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH query [SUBJECT] [FLAGS]
```

| Subject | Output |
|---|---|
| none | Every entity, one `name`, `kind`, `defined_in`, `declared_in` line each, grouped by kind. `--closure-only`, `--external-only`, `--api-only` and `--file` narrow it. |
| `functions`, `globals`, `macros`, `function_pointers`, `typedefs` | Records of that kind: signatures, callers and callees, and findings. A function pointer is a typedef declaring one, its aliases folded in, or one written inline, named by its signature. A typedef is one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer. |
| `structs`, `unions`, `enums` | Records of that kind: fields, casts, users, and findings. |
| `files` | The closure, external, and API file sets. |
| `dag` | Dependency closures, graph layers, and cycle twins. |

Common flags:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Select entities by name. Without it, a kind's subject lists its names. |
| `--file FILE ...` | Narrow named entities to those defined in these files. |
| `--closure-only`, `--external-only` | Keep entities defined in the closure's files, or the external ones it reaches. |
| `--api-only` | Keep entities the `api_headers` publish. |
| `--update FINDINGS` | Submit findings for one named entity (`-` reads stdin). |
| `--in-tree`, `--out-of-tree` | Listing only: keep entities defined inside, or outside, the repository. |

Struct, union and enum views (one `--name`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--fields` | Print the declared fields and their records. |
| `--lifecycle-ops` | Print the routines that drop, dispose, clone, or construct the type. |
| `--users` | Print every function that uses the type, and for an enum every global and macro that names one of its constants. |
| `--field-touchers` | Print each field and the functions that access it. |
| `--layout-users` | Print every function, global and aggregate that depends on the type's layout, with the sites of each use. |
| `--raw-sites` | Print every function that allocates or frees the type with a raw routine (a lifecycle role on a `void *`, in the ownership store), with each site. With `--unresolved` and no `--name`: the raw sites on type-erased values no table types. |

Function searches (`--callees` and `--callers` also take a global, macro or typedef):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--taking SPEC` | Find functions with an argument of type `SPEC` (a type, `void`, or `string`). |
| `--returning SPEC` | Find functions that return a pointer of type `SPEC`. |
| `--lifetime-for SPEC` | Find the submitted lifecycle routines acting on `SPEC`. |
| `--calling FN,...` | With `--taking` or `--returning`, keep functions that reach one of `FN`. |
| `--callees`, `--callers` | Walk the call graph forward or backward from `--name`. |
| `--depth N` | Hop limit for the walks above; default `1`. |
| `--array` | Keep matches classified as arrays. |

Graph views (`query dag`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Print the dependency closure of the named nodes. |
| `--depth N` | Limit the closure to `N` hops. |
| `--layer N` | Print every node in layer `N`. |
| `--scc hi-deps\|lo-deps` | With `--name`, print the cycle twins recorded in `fallback` or `back_fill`. |
| `--loc` | Report estimated lines of code. |
| `--kind KIND` | With `--name`, keep its nodes of this kind (`function`, `struct`, ...). A name that names several nodes resolves to all of them, listed under `matches` with their kinds and files. |
| `--api-headers-only` | Use the public-signature graph. |

Examples:

```sh
# List everything the headers publish, by kind.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json query --api-only

# Show one type's fields.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query structs --name widget_st --fields

# Find functions that take widget_st and reach widget_release within 3 calls.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query functions --taking widget_st --calling widget_release --depth 3

# Show the dependencies of widget_new.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query dag --name widget_new --depth 1
```

Each subject's `--help` lists its complete flags.

A type or symbol record has two parts: `composed`, which Wavefront derives
from the code, and `findings`, which users fill. `findings` lists every slot
the entity accepts, in the shape `--update` takes, so a user can fill it in
and submit it. See [`docs/artifacts/findings.md`](docs/artifacts/findings.md)
and [`examples/findings.json`](examples/findings.json).

### 3. Schedule

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH schedule --output PATH [FLAGS]
```

A schedule orders every unit of the config's closure, in the groups its
[`modules`](docs/scoping.md#modules) make, keeps its
[`schedule_seeds`](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds) and every unit they depend
on, and emits one wave per layer of each module. A unit no module claims
goes in a wave of the first module that needs it, ahead of the wave that
does, or in a wave of its own when it is a seed, or what only such a seed
needs. A narrow schedule keeps the order and cuts of the whole
closure, so a consumer can schedule parts of a library in turn without
changing the order. Each unit carries its module, its `defined_in` and
`declared_in` files, and the statistics a consumer weighs its work by. A
struct, union or enum also carries the point after which none of its layout
users is left to process, `opaque_after`, and a struct or union the point
after which no C allocates or frees it with a raw routine,
`memory_unmanaged_after`; a function, global, macro, function pointer or
typedef the point after which none of its referrers is, `unreferenced_after`
([Release points](docs/batching.md#release-points)).

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|---|---:|---|
| `--output PATH` | | Required. Output file; its directory must exist. |
| `--api-headers-only` | | Schedule the public API from the public-signature graph. |
| `--max-types N` | none | Types per type batch. |
| `--min-fields N` | none | Declared fields that close a type batch. |
| `--max-syms N` | none | Symbols per symbol batch. |
| `--max-loc N` | none | Body lines per symbol batch; `0` disables the limit. |

Without a cap, a wave holds two batches, its types and generator macros, then
everything else, for the consumer to split.

Example:

```sh
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json schedule \
  --api-headers-only --output /src/widget/schedule.json
```

See [`examples/schedule.json`](examples/schedule.json) for the output.

## Documentation

| Document | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`docs/graph.md`](docs/graph.md) | The dependency graph: nodes, edges, type erasure, cycles, polymorphism, and limitations. |
| [`docs/scoping.md`](docs/scoping.md) | The closure, modules, the schedule seeds, closure and external entities, the API view, and default and API modes. |
| [`docs/batching.md`](docs/batching.md) | Units, their order, waves, batch caps, and release points. |
| [`docs/pointer-properties.md`](docs/pointer-properties.md) | The pointer properties recorded in the ownership store. |
| [`docs/type-lifecycle.md`](docs/type-lifecycle.md) | Lifecycle roles, and how to find the routines that play them. |
| [`docs/artifacts/`](docs/artifacts/) | Field reference for type and symbol records, findings, the ownership store, schedules, and T3 tables. |

## Tests

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

The default suite runs no CodeQL. A fixture's tests that compose, query or
schedule it read its committed tables, `tests/fixtures/<name>/codeql/`. The
tests that build each fixture's database and run the queries, checking the
queries' golden tables and that the committed tables are current, are
opt-in, and pass before a change to a query or a fixture's C lands:

```sh
WAVEFRONT_CODEQL_TESTS=1 PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

After such a change, re-extract the committed tables and review their diff:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python tests/regenerate_tables.py [FIXTURE ...]
```

- Marius Momeu, marius.momeu@berkeley.edu

# Pointer properties

A C pointer type states where a pointer points, but not how much it points
at, who releases it, or whether it may be null. A user records those facts
as a pointer's properties, in the ownership store
([`artifacts/ownership-store.md`](artifacts/ownership-store.md)). A Rust
translation reads them to choose the pointer's Rust type: a reference, a
slice, a string, an owning box, an `Option`.

## Where pointers occur

The same block of properties, `ptr`, describes a pointer wherever it occurs:

| site | record | ownership is relative to |
|---|---|---|
| parameter | `ptr_args[].ptr` on a function or callback | the call: the callee takes it, or borrows it |
| return | `ptr_ret.ptr` on a function or callback | the call: the caller receives it, or borrows it |
| field | `fields[].ptr` on a type | the enclosing struct |
| global | `ptr` on a global | the program |

A composed record carries `ptr: null` until a user submits a block, so
`null` means the pointer has not been analyzed. A submitted block replaces
the previous one entirely and must be complete.

## Shape

Three properties state what the pointer points at. A pointer sets at least
one of them, and may set several when different execution paths use it
differently.

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `scalar` | `null`, `{by_val: true}`, or `{by_ref: {owned, borrowed}}` | On some path the pointer refers to a single pointee: one value (`by_val`, an ordinary `T *`), or one pointer (`by_ref`, a `T **` such as an out-parameter). |
| `array` | `null`, `{by_val: true}`, or `{by_ref: {owned, borrowed}}` | On some path the pointer refers to a buffer: of values (`by_val`), or of pointers (`by_ref`, a container). |
| `string` | `true` or `false` | On some path the pointer refers to a NUL-terminated string. |

Under `by_ref`, `owned` and `borrowed` describe the inner pointers, the
pointee of a `T **` or the elements of a container, with the same
meaning as at the top level. The top-level `owned` and `borrowed` then
describe the outer pointer. `scalar.by_ref` and `array.by_ref` differ only
in how many inner pointers there are.

## Ownership

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `owned` | `true` or `false` | Whoever holds the pointer must release it. A parameter's ownership passes to the callee; a return's passes to the caller; a field's belongs to the struct. |
| `borrowed` | `null` or `{lifetime}` | The pointer is valid only while another entity is; `lifetime` names it. |

A pointer is owned, borrowed, or both; never neither. Both are set when
ownership depends on the path taken: owned on one, borrowed on another. The
same holds for each `by_ref` inner pointer.

A borrowed lifetime names its source in the vocabulary of the site:

| site | sources |
|---|---|
| parameter, return | `arg:<name>`, `arg:<name>-><path>`, `static`, `other` |
| field | `self` (the enclosing struct), `field:<name>` (a sibling field's storage), `static`, `other` |
| global | `static`, `other` |

A parameter is always named by its name, never by its position: in an
`arg:<name>` lifetime, and as the key of `ptr_args` in a submission. A
pointer that is read only during the call borrows from itself:
`arg:<its own name>`.

## Access

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nullable` | `true` or `false` | The pointer may be `NULL`. |
| `mutable` | `true`, `false`, or `null` | Code writes through the pointer. A `const` pointee forces `false`; `null` only when it cannot be determined, as for an external function with no body. |
| `note` | text | The reasoning behind the block, and its gaps and corner cases. |

## Invariants

`query --update` rejects a block, and applies nothing, unless:

- `scalar` and `array` are each `null` or exactly one of `by_val` and
  `by_ref`;
- at least one of `scalar`, `array` and `string` is set;
- `string` and `owned` are booleans, never `null`;
- the pointer, and each `by_ref` inner pointer, is owned or borrowed;
- a borrowed pointer has a lifetime, and an `arg:<name>` lifetime names a
  parameter of the same symbol;
- a `const` pointee has `mutable` other than `true`;
- `ptr_ret` is set only on a symbol that returns a pointer.

## Related bindings

Two more judgements sit beside `ptr` on a field or a global, because they
apply to non-pointer data as well:

- `refcount` marks the one field that stores its type's reference count
  ([`type-lifecycle.md`](type-lifecycle.md));
- `locked_by` names the lock that guards a field or global, and the
  routines that acquire and release it: `{lock, lock_op, unlock_op}`.
# Type lifecycle

A type's lifecycle is the set of routines that create, copy and release its
objects. C states none of it: `widget_free` is a function like any other.
A user identifies these routines and records them in the ownership store
([`artifacts/ownership-store.md`](artifacts/ownership-store.md)), so a Rust
translation can implement construction, `Clone` and `Drop` with them.

## What the store holds

A lifecycle is recorded on the routines, not on the type. Each routine's
symbol record carries a `lifetime` block: the role it plays and the
parameter it acts on (`for`), or `"return"` for a constructor that returns
the new object. Field schema: [`artifacts/findings.md`](artifacts/findings.md#lifetime).

| role | the routine |
|---|---|
| `is_dropper` | frees the object's own storage: a full destructor. The argument must be owned. |
| `is_disposer` | frees what the object's fields own, but keeps the object's storage: a cleanup or reset that leaves it reusable. |
| `is_cloner` | copies the object: `deep`, a new independent allocation, or `upref`, a reference-count increment that returns the same object. The argument must be borrowed. |
| `is_constructor` | produces an object: `alloc`, a new object the caller owns, returned or stored through a `T **` out-parameter; or `init`, initialization of caller-provided storage in place. |

A routine is a dropper or a disposer, never both. A constructor plays no
other role. A routine that returns storage a separate `init` must still
complete is an allocator, not an `alloc` constructor.

One field per type may be marked `refcount`: the field an up-ref increments
and a down-ref decrements. A reference-counted type is released by its
down-ref and copied by its up-ref; any other type by its dropper and deep
cloner.

The lifecycle is read back from the routines:

- `query structs --name T --lifecycle-ops` lists the routines acting on `T`,
  lifecycle roles first;
- `query functions --lifetime-for T` lists the routines with a role on `T`,
  `void` or `string`.

Lifecycle roles never change the dependency graph
([`graph.md`](graph.md#nodes)) or the order a schedule is made in. A
schedule reads only the `void` roles below, for its items' `memory_unmanaged_after`
([`batching.md`](batching.md#raw-sites)): the raw routines are established
while planning, before the schedule is made.

## Raw lifetimes: `void` and `string`

Two lifecycles belong to no type. The `void` lifecycle covers untyped
memory (`void *`): the allocators, releasers and copiers of raw bytes. The
`string` lifecycle covers NUL-terminated strings. Neither is a node of the
graph, so no schedule holds them: a consumer that binds them schedules them
itself, before the types whose lifecycles build on them, since a type's
routines release its memory through the raw ones.

## How to discover lifecycle routines

The routines worth recording are those that release, dispose of, copy or
construct storage: heap allocations, and the fields of a type embedded by
value or held on the stack. Record a routine when more than one caller uses
it, or when the API publishes it. A helper that only lifecycle routines
call need not be recorded. `query functions --callers` and `--callees` show
who uses a routine.

### `void`

1. Start from the C library: `free`, `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `mmap`,
   `munmap`, `memcpy`, `memmove`, `strdup`, `strndup`.
2. Find the project's own routines that call them, and follow callers a few
   hops further for more specialized ones.
3. Keep releasers and copiers that take a `void *` (`--taking void`).
4. Find allocators by their return, since `malloc(size_t)` takes no
   `void *`: `--returning void --calling malloc,calloc --depth N`. Record
   each as an `alloc` constructor, and note whether it zeroes the memory.
5. Do not record a `realloc`-style routine as a constructor: it releases
   and allocates the same storage, and a constructor plays no other role.

Include routines that handle arrays as well as single objects.

### `string`

1. Find routines that take a `char *`, `unsigned char *`, `uint8_t *` or a
   similar character pointer and call one of the `void` routines, then
   follow callers a few hops further.
2. Check the `void` routines as well: some of them also release or copy
   strings, and those are recorded for `string` too.
3. Find constructors with `--returning string`: formatters, tokenizers and
   path joiners that return a new string. Record each as an `alloc`
   constructor.
4. Record a routine that copies a string argument as a cloner, not a
   constructor. A raw allocator stays in the `void` lifecycle even when its
   memory later holds a string, because it does not return one.

### A type `T`

1. Find routines that take a `T *` (`--taking T`) and call one of the
   `void` routines.
2. Follow callers a few hops further to the top-level droppers, disposers
   and cloners, which often reach the raw routines through helpers.
3. Find constructors: `alloc` ones return a `T *` (`--returning T`) or store
   it through a `T **` (`--taking T`, depth 2); `init` ones fill a
   caller's `T *` in place.
4. For a plain type released only as part of an enclosing type, record the
   enclosing type's disposer.

Include routines that handle arrays as well as single objects. Submit the
roles with `query functions --update`, on each routine; a type's own record
holds no lifecycle.

# Wavefront

Wavefront analyzes a C codebase and schedules its units in dependency order
for translation to Rust. It extracts entities and dependencies with CodeQL,
builds a cycle-free dependency graph of the codebase's types and symbols, and
packs that graph into ordered waves of batches. Each batch can be translated
once the waves before it are complete.

Wavefront keeps its analysis simple: it infers facts from the codebase without
data-flow or points-to analysis. It is built for neuro-symbolic workflows, in
which human or LLM reasoning complements its static facts. You can state the
polymorphic and type-erased edges it cannot infer; Wavefront loads them into
the dependency graph, and its schedules order units by them. You can also
record pointer-level ownership and lifecycle properties for each type and
symbol, which Wavefront returns with their records.

## Requirements

- Python 3.13 or newer
- The [CodeQL CLI](https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries), on `PATH`

## Installation

```sh
git clone https://github.com/crustify-rs/wavefront.git
cd wavefront
python -m pip install -e .
codeql pack install src/
```

## Usage

```text
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH COMMAND ...
```

`REPO_ROOT` is the root of the C repository. `--config` names its
`wavefront-config.json`; a relative path is resolved from `REPO_ROOT`.

### Configuration

```json
{
  "state_dir": ".wavefront",
  "closure": {
    "impl_files": {"included": ["src/"], "excluded": ["src/tests/"]},
    "api_headers": {"included": ["include/widget.h"]}
  },
  "modules": [
    {"name": "src/mem.c", "files": ["src/mem.c", "src/mem.h"]},
    {"name": "src/widget.c", "files": ["src/widget.c", "include/widget.h"]}
  ],
  "schedule_seeds": ["include/widget.h"],
  "t3_dir": "t3"
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state_dir` | Directory for the CodeQL database and tables, ownership findings, and caches. |
| `closure` | The program Wavefront analyzes, for its graph, queries and usage counts: `impl_files`, the sources and private headers that implement it, and `api_headers`, the headers that publish its API, each `included` files and directories, less what `excluded` matches. See [Files](docs/scoping.md#files). |
| `modules` | Optional. Module records, `{name, files}`, each file entry as in `schedule_seeds`: a module is a named group of files and items, typically a TU with its headers, unrelated to C++20 modules. A schedule orders each module's units together, the modules in dependency order with their cycles cut. A unit no module claims is ordered alone. See [Modules](docs/scoping.md#modules). |
| `schedule_seeds` | Optional. What `wavefront schedule` starts from: a list of file entries, each seeding what its file defines or declares; a schedule holds its seeds and what they depend on. A file entry is a path, a directory written with a trailing slash, or `{path, items}` whose `included` and `excluded` items, each `{name, kind}`, narrow what it seeds. Without it, every unit of the closure. See [Schedule seeds](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds). |
| `t3_dir` | Optional. Directory, relative to `state_dir`, holding the T3 tables ([`examples/t3/`](examples/t3/)). |

Paths are relative to `REPO_ROOT`. A trailing slash selects a directory
recursively, in `included` and `excluded` alike; `excluded` is optional. See [`examples/wavefront-config.json`](examples/wavefront-config.json).

### 1. Extract

Build the project under CodeQL, then extract the T1 (entity) and T2 (edge)
tables into `<state_dir>/codeql/`:

```sh
codeql database create REPO_ROOT/.wavefront/codeql/db \
  --language=cpp --source-root=REPO_ROOT --command="make -j"
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config wavefront-config.json extract-ql
```

Run `extract-ql` again only when the database changes.

### 2. Query

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH query [SUBJECT] [FLAGS]
```

| Subject | Output |
|---|---|
| none | Every entity, one `name`, `kind`, `defined_in`, `declared_in` line each, grouped by kind. `--closure-only`, `--external-only`, `--api-only` and `--file` narrow it. |
| `functions`, `globals`, `macros`, `function_pointers`, `typedefs` | Records of that kind: signatures, callers and callees, and findings. A function pointer is a typedef declaring one, its aliases folded in, or one written inline, named by its signature. A typedef is one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer. |
| `structs`, `unions`, `enums` | Records of that kind: fields, casts, users, and findings. |
| `files` | The closure, external, and API file sets. |
| `dag` | Dependency closures, graph layers, and cycle twins. |

Common flags:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Select entities by name. Without it, a kind's subject lists its names. |
| `--file FILE ...` | Narrow named entities to those defined in these files. |
| `--closure-only`, `--external-only` | Keep entities defined in the closure's files, or the external ones it reaches. |
| `--api-only` | Keep entities the `api_headers` publish. |
| `--update FINDINGS` | Submit findings for one named entity (`-` reads stdin). |
| `--in-tree`, `--out-of-tree` | Listing only: keep entities defined inside, or outside, the repository. |

Struct, union and enum views (one `--name`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--fields` | Print the declared fields and their records. |
| `--lifecycle-ops` | Print the routines that drop, dispose, clone, or construct the type. |
| `--users` | Print every function that uses the type, and for an enum every global and macro that names one of its constants. |
| `--field-touchers` | Print each field and the functions that access it. |
| `--layout-users` | Print every function, global and aggregate that depends on the type's layout, with the sites of each use. |
| `--raw-sites` | Print every function that allocates or frees the type with a raw routine (a lifecycle role on a `void *`, in the ownership store), with each site. With `--unresolved` and no `--name`: the raw sites on type-erased values no table types. |

Function searches (`--callees` and `--callers` also take a global, macro or typedef):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--taking SPEC` | Find functions with an argument of type `SPEC` (a type, `void`, or `string`). |
| `--returning SPEC` | Find functions that return a pointer of type `SPEC`. |
| `--lifetime-for SPEC` | Find the submitted lifecycle routines acting on `SPEC`. |
| `--calling FN,...` | With `--taking` or `--returning`, keep functions that reach one of `FN`. |
| `--callees`, `--callers` | Walk the call graph forward or backward from `--name`. |
| `--depth N` | Hop limit for the walks above; default `1`. |
| `--array` | Keep matches classified as arrays. |

Graph views (`query dag`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Print the dependency closure of the named nodes. |
| `--depth N` | Limit the closure to `N` hops. |
| `--layer N` | Print every node in layer `N`. |
| `--scc hi-deps\|lo-deps` | With `--name`, print the cycle twins recorded in `fallback` or `back_fill`. |
| `--loc` | Report estimated lines of code. |
| `--kind KIND` | With `--name`, keep its nodes of this kind (`function`, `struct`, ...). A name that names several nodes resolves to all of them, listed under `matches` with their kinds and files. |
| `--api-headers-only` | Use the public-signature graph. |

Examples:

```sh
# List everything the headers publish, by kind.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json query --api-only

# Show one type's fields.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query structs --name widget_st --fields

# Find functions that take widget_st and reach widget_release within 3 calls.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query functions --taking widget_st --calling widget_release --depth 3

# Show the dependencies of widget_new.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query dag --name widget_new --depth 1
```

Each subject's `--help` lists its complete flags.

A type or symbol record has two parts: `composed`, which Wavefront derives
from the code, and `findings`, which users fill. `findings` lists every slot
the entity accepts, in the shape `--update` takes, so a user can fill it in
and submit it. See [`docs/artifacts/findings.md`](docs/artifacts/findings.md)
and [`examples/findings.json`](examples/findings.json).

### 3. Schedule

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH schedule --output PATH [FLAGS]
```

A schedule orders every unit of the config's closure, in the groups its
[`modules`](docs/scoping.md#modules) make, keeps its
[`schedule_seeds`](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds) and every unit they depend
on, and emits one wave per layer of each module. A unit no module claims
goes in a wave of the first module that needs it, ahead of the wave that
does, or in a wave of its own when it is a seed, or what only such a seed
needs. A narrow schedule keeps the order and cuts of the whole
closure, so a consumer can schedule parts of a library in turn without
changing the order. Each unit carries its module, its `defined_in` and
`declared_in` files, and the statistics a consumer weighs its work by. A
struct, union or enum also carries the point after which none of its layout
users is left to process, `opaque_after`, and a struct or union the point
after which no C allocates or frees it with a raw routine,
`memory_unmanaged_after`; a function, global, macro, function pointer or
typedef the point after which none of its referrers is, `unreferenced_after`
([Release points](docs/batching.md#release-points)).

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|---|---:|---|
| `--output PATH` | | Required. Output file; its directory must exist. |
| `--api-headers-only` | | Schedule the public API from the public-signature graph. |
| `--max-types N` | none | Types per type batch. |
| `--min-fields N` | none | Declared fields that close a type batch. |
| `--max-syms N` | none | Symbols per symbol batch. |
| `--max-loc N` | none | Body lines per symbol batch; `0` disables the limit. |

Without a cap, a wave holds two batches, its types and generator macros, then
everything else, for the consumer to split.

Example:

```sh
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json schedule \
  --api-headers-only --output /src/widget/schedule.json
```

See [`examples/schedule.json`](examples/schedule.json) for the output.

## Documentation

| Document | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`docs/graph.md`](docs/graph.md) | The dependency graph: nodes, edges, type erasure, cycles, polymorphism, and limitations. |
| [`docs/scoping.md`](docs/scoping.md) | The closure, modules, the schedule seeds, closure and external entities, the API view, and default and API modes. |
| [`docs/batching.md`](docs/batching.md) | Units, their order, waves, batch caps, and release points. |
| [`docs/pointer-properties.md`](docs/pointer-properties.md) | The pointer properties recorded in the ownership store. |
| [`docs/type-lifecycle.md`](docs/type-lifecycle.md) | Lifecycle roles, and how to find the routines that play them. |
| [`docs/artifacts/`](docs/artifacts/) | Field reference for type and symbol records, findings, the ownership store, schedules, and T3 tables. |

## Tests

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

The default suite runs no CodeQL. A fixture's tests that compose, query or
schedule it read its committed tables, `tests/fixtures/<name>/codeql/`. The
tests that build each fixture's database and run the queries, checking the
queries' golden tables and that the committed tables are current, are
opt-in, and pass before a change to a query or a fixture's C lands:

```sh
WAVEFRONT_CODEQL_TESTS=1 PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

After such a change, re-extract the committed tables and review their diff:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python tests/regenerate_tables.py [FIXTURE ...]
```

# Pointer properties

A C pointer type states where a pointer points, but not how much it points
at, who releases it, or whether it may be null. A user records those facts
as a pointer's properties, in the ownership store
([`artifacts/ownership-store.md`](artifacts/ownership-store.md)). A Rust
translation reads them to choose the pointer's Rust type: a reference, a
slice, a string, an owning box, an `Option`.

## Where pointers occur

The same block of properties, `ptr`, describes a pointer wherever it occurs:

| site | record | ownership is relative to |
|---|---|---|
| parameter | `ptr_args[].ptr` on a function or callback | the call: the callee takes it, or borrows it |
| return | `ptr_ret.ptr` on a function or callback | the call: the caller receives it, or borrows it |
| field | `fields[].ptr` on a type | the enclosing struct |
| global | `ptr` on a global | the program |

A composed record carries `ptr: null` until a user submits a block, so
`null` means the pointer has not been analyzed. A submitted block replaces
the previous one entirely and must be complete.

## Shape

Three properties state what the pointer points at. A pointer sets at least
one of them, and may set several when different execution paths use it
differently.

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `scalar` | `null`, `{by_val: true}`, or `{by_ref: {owned, borrowed}}` | On some path the pointer refers to a single pointee: one value (`by_val`, an ordinary `T *`), or one pointer (`by_ref`, a `T **` such as an out-parameter). |
| `array` | `null`, `{by_val: true}`, or `{by_ref: {owned, borrowed}}` | On some path the pointer refers to a buffer: of values (`by_val`), or of pointers (`by_ref`, a container). |
| `string` | `true` or `false` | On some path the pointer refers to a NUL-terminated string. |

Under `by_ref`, `owned` and `borrowed` describe the inner pointers, the
pointee of a `T **` or the elements of a container, with the same
meaning as at the top level. The top-level `owned` and `borrowed` then
describe the outer pointer. `scalar.by_ref` and `array.by_ref` differ only
in how many inner pointers there are.

## Ownership

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `owned` | `true` or `false` | Whoever holds the pointer must release it. A parameter's ownership passes to the callee; a return's passes to the caller; a field's belongs to the struct. |
| `borrowed` | `null` or `{lifetime}` | The pointer is valid only while another entity is; `lifetime` names it. |

A pointer is owned, borrowed, or both; never neither. Both are set when
ownership depends on the path taken: owned on one, borrowed on another. The
same holds for each `by_ref` inner pointer.

A borrowed lifetime names its source in the vocabulary of the site:

| site | sources |
|---|---|
| parameter, return | `arg:<name>`, `arg:<name>-><path>`, `static`, `other` |
| field | `self` (the enclosing struct), `field:<name>` (a sibling field's storage), `static`, `other` |
| global | `static`, `other` |

A parameter is always named by its name, never by its position: in an
`arg:<name>` lifetime, and as the key of `ptr_args` in a submission. A
pointer that is read only during the call borrows from itself:
`arg:<its own name>`.

## Access

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nullable` | `true` or `false` | The pointer may be `NULL`. |
| `mutable` | `true`, `false`, or `null` | Code writes through the pointer. A `const` pointee forces `false`; `null` only when it cannot be determined, as for an external function with no body. |
| `note` | text | The reasoning behind the block, and its gaps and corner cases. |

## Invariants

`query --update` rejects a block, and applies nothing, unless:

- `scalar` and `array` are each `null` or exactly one of `by_val` and
  `by_ref`;
- at least one of `scalar`, `array` and `string` is set;
- `string` and `owned` are booleans, never `null`;
- the pointer, and each `by_ref` inner pointer, is owned or borrowed;
- a borrowed pointer has a lifetime, and an `arg:<name>` lifetime names a
  parameter of the same symbol;
- a `const` pointee has `mutable` other than `true`;

   strings, and those are recorded for `string` too.

   constructor.

   constructor. A raw allocator stays in the `void` lifecycle even when its
   memory later holds a string, because it does not return one.

### A type `T`

1. Find routines that take a `T *` (`--taking T`) and call one of the
   `void` routines.
2. Follow callers a few hops further to the top-level droppers, disposers
   and cloners, which often reach the raw routines through helpers.

   enclosing type's disposer.
